title: Which side of the plane to sit on flying to Tenerife
author: Matt
intro: For the best chance of seeing Mount Teide as you land at Tenerife South, sit on the left side of the plane. Here's why that usually works, when the wind flips it, and where to sit on the way home.
seo_title: Flying to Tenerife: sit on the left for Teide (usually)
seo_description: Usually the left side (seat A) for Mount Teide as you land at Tenerife South. Why the wind can flip it, which seats to avoid and the best side flying home.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
**Sit on the left side of the plane** for the best chance of seeing Mount Teide as you land at Tenerife South. On most UK holiday flights, that means a window seat lettered **A**.

It isn't a guarantee. The view depends on which way the plane lands, which depends on the wind, and Teide is sometimes hidden in cloud. But the left side is the better bet on most days, for reasons that are easy to understand.

sections.heading: Why the left side usually wins
sections.text:
Tenerife South Airport has one runway, running roughly south-west to north-east along the island's southern coast. Planes land into the wind, and Tenerife's usual trade winds blow from the north-east. So most of the time, planes land heading north-east, coming in over the sea from the south-west.

Teide sits in the middle of the island, north-west of the airport. On that usual approach, the island and the mountain rise up on your **left**, while the right side looks out over the sea, sometimes towards Gran Canaria in the distance.

At 3,715 metres, Teide is the highest mountain in Spain. On a clear day you can see its summit from far out at sea, often sticking up above a layer of cloud.

sections.heading: When the right side is better
sections.text:
Now and then the wind changes direction, and planes land the other way, heading south-west and coming in from the east. On those days the mountain is on your **right**.

There's no way to know which way you'll land when you book your seat. Some of the flight before the final approach may also show the island on the right as the plane lines up, so it's worth looking out of both sides as you descend.

If you're flying into **Tenerife North** instead, this advice doesn't apply. Most UK holiday flights use Tenerife South, but check your booking.

sections.heading: Which seats to choose
sections.text:
Most UK holiday flights to Tenerife use narrow-body aircraft like the Boeing 737 or Airbus A320, with seats lettered A to F:

- **A** is the left window, and **F** is the right window.
- **Avoid seats over the wing**, roughly rows 10 to 20 on most of these planes. The wing blocks much of the view of the ground.
- **Seats near the front** have the clearest view and are first off the plane, but often cost more.
- **Seats behind the wing** are usually cheaper and give a good view, though the engine can be in the way.

If you'd rather not pay to choose a seat, try asking at bag drop. Window seats on the left are sometimes still free.

sections.heading: On the way home
sections.text:
Planes usually take off heading north-east too, for the same reason. As you climb away from the coast, the island is on your left, and you may get a final look at Teide before the plane turns north for the UK.

It's less predictable than the landing, though, because the plane can turn quite quickly. If you sat on the left on the way out, it's worth trying the right on the way home for a different view, perhaps of Gran Canaria.

sections.heading: What else you might see
sections.text:
UK flights to Tenerife take about four to four and a half hours. Much of that is over the Atlantic, but on a clear day you may spot the coast of Portugal or Spain early on, and later Madeira or the other Canary Islands as you head south.

La Gomera, Tenerife's small, steep neighbour to the west, is often visible as you come in to land from the south-west. If you're staying on the island, it's an easy day trip by ferry from Los Cristianos.

sections.heading: Where could you go from Tenerife?
sections.text:
Tenerife is one of the most reliable places in Europe for winter sun. Our [Tenerife guide](/destinations/tenerife) covers where to stay and when it's warmest. If you're still choosing an island, our [Madeira or Tenerife](/blog/madeira-or-tenerife) post compares the two, and our guides to [Gran Canaria](/destinations/gran-canaria) and [Lanzarote](/destinations/lanzarote) cover the alternatives. For more ideas, see [winter sun with no jet lag](/blog/winter-sun-with-no-jet-lag).

If your group can't agree where to go, our guide to [how to decide where to go on holiday](/how-to-decide-where-to-go-on-holiday) shows a fair way to pick. For seats on other routes, read [which side of the plane to sit on](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on).

faqs.question: Which side of the plane is best for Mount Teide?
faqs.answer: The left side is usually best when landing at Tenerife South, because planes normally approach from the south-west with the island on the left. If the wind changes and planes land the other way, the right side is better.

faqs.question: Can you see Mount Teide from the plane?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. At 3,715 metres it's usually visible from far out at sea, sometimes poking above the clouds. Cloud can hide it completely on some days.

faqs.question: Is seat A on the left of the plane?
faqs.answer: Yes. On narrow-body planes like the Boeing 737 and Airbus A320, seat A is the left window and seat F is the right window.

faqs.question: How long is the flight from the UK to Tenerife?
faqs.answer: About four to four and a half hours from most UK airports.
